title: Why should they believe you?
principle: Let buyers check your promise for themselves.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a man named Elisha Otis. In the 1850s, people in America were scared of lifts. If the rope broke, the lift fell. Otis had built a lift with a safety brake. But every seller said "my lift is safe", so nobody listened.

screens.title: The show
screens.text: So in 1854, at a big fair in New York, Otis stood on an open lift platform, high above a crowd. Then he had the rope cut. The platform dropped a little, and stopped. His brake had caught it. He had bet his own life on his claim.

screens.prompt: Otis had said "my lift is safe" for a long time, and few believed him. Why do you think the show worked?

options.label: A big fair gave him a big crowd
Nobody would risk his life on a lie

screens.why: The crowd helped, but here's the real reason. A liar would never stand on that platform. The show would have cost Otis his life if his claim were false, so people believed it.

screens.title: Costly signals
screens.text: Anyone can say "best quality". Words cost nothing, so buyers don't believe them. Buyers believe proof that would cost a liar a lot. This is called a costly signal. Otis could never have faked standing on that platform.

screens.title: Let them check
screens.text: A small shop doesn't need to risk its life. The easiest costly signal is to let buyers check the claim themselves. A dairy tests the milk's fat in front of you. A liar can't do that. When buyers can check, they don't need to trust you.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Otis sold lifts, but your bakery has the same problem with words. It's the first week of September. Many Jain families in the new colony want eggless cakes. Your cakes really are eggless, and they cost ₹850. But families ask, "How do we know?"

screens.prompt: Families ask how they can know your ₹850 cake is really eggless. Which answer will they believe most?

options.label: "100% eggless, I promise" on every post
Five happy customers post reviews for you
Families can watch their own cake baked, live on video

screens.why: Yes. On a live video, families watch their own cake being made. They don't have to trust your words.

wrong.a: Anyone can write "I promise". It costs nothing, so a family that was fooled before won't believe it. A live video lets them see for themselves.
wrong.b: Reviews help, and you'll learn more about them soon. But a review can't prove there's no egg in this family's cake. A live video of their own cake lets them check.

screens.prompt: Your sister: "Spend ₹8,000 on an ad saying 'pure eggless'." Your friend: "Pay ₹5,000 if a food lab ever finds egg." Who's right?
screens.why: Right. Any family can send a slice to a lab. The ₹5,000 promise costs you nothing if you're honest, but it would ruin a liar. That's why families believe it. A liar could pay for the same ad.

wrong.a: The ad does cost money, but a liar could pay ₹8,000 for the same ad. Your friend's promise would only cost a liar, so families believe it.
wrong.c: Plain words don't work, but this promise isn't plain words. It would cost a liar ₹5,000 each time, so families believe it.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six things a baker might do. For each one, tell me: can buyers check it, or must they trust you?

items.text: A live video of the cake being baked
"Made with love" printed on the box
Every ingredient listed, with the packs shown
A slice of the same cake to taste before you pay

screens.why: A video, the packs on show and a taste before paying are things buyers can check for themselves. "Made with love", "freshest" and "always happy" cost nothing to say, so buyers must just trust you.

screens.setup: A week later, a chain bakery opens near the colony. Its cakes cost ₹700, and its sign says "pure butter". Your real-butter cakes cost ₹400 to make and sell for ₹850. You sell 20 a week. A mother says, "They say butter too, and they're cheaper."
screens.question: What do you do?

options.label: Cut your cake to ₹700 to match them
options.outcome: You still sell 20 cakes a week, but each now leaves you ₹300, not ₹450. That's ₹6,000 a week, not ₹9,000. Families still can't tell your butter from theirs.
options.why: A price cut didn't prove anything. You lost ₹3,000 a week and gave buyers no way to see the difference.
options.better: Let families check: show the butter packs and the baking.

options.label: Ask 10 happy buyers to post "real butter" reviews
options.outcome: Families have heard "pure butter" from both of you. 3 of your 20 weekly buyers try the chain. You sell 17 cakes, leaving you ₹7,650 a week.
options.why: You kept your price, but reviews just repeated your words, and the chain has happy buyers too. Nothing showed which claim was true.
options.better: Let families check: show the butter packs and the baking.

options.label: Show the butter packs in every baking video
options.outcome: Families see the butter packs and the bill in every video. A mother asks the chain shop to show the same. It has nothing to show. You keep all 20 weekly buyers at ₹850, leaving you ₹9,000 a week.
options.why: You gave proof that buyers could check. Now the chain's claim looks weak next to yours.

screens.text: Words cost ___, so buyers believe proof they can ___ for themselves.
screens.why: Exactly. Otis let the crowd see the brake catch. You let families watch their own cake and see the butter. Proof they can check is a costly signal any honest shop can afford.

summary: Costly signalling: proof that would cost a liar a lot is believed. Cheap words are not.
A costly ad isn't a costly signal. A liar can pay for an ad too.
Let buyers check your claim themselves: show the baking, the packs, the date.

cards.front: A ghee seller wants buyers to believe it's pure. What works best?
options: Melt a spoon so buyers can smell and taste it
cards.back: Let buyers check the claim themselves. Words cost nothing, so they prove nothing.

cards.front: Which promise is a costly signal?
options: ₹5,000 to anyone who finds a fault
cards.back: A costly signal costs only a liar. Anyone, honest or not, can pay for an ad.

cards.front: A rival copies your claim, "pure butter". How do you show yours is true?
options: Show the butter packs and the baking
cards.back: When both say the same words, the one who shows proof wins.
